common_name: Autumn Crisp Apple (Cornell Breeding-Line Parent of RubyFrost)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator within range for good fruit set. Autumn Crisp was bred at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva and is best known today as one of the two parents (crossed with Braeburn) of the Cornell-released RubyFrost apple, though it is still grown in its own right in some Northeastern orchards.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Autumn Crisp is a Cornell University-bred apple from the Geneva, New York breeding program, grown today mainly by collectors and a few Northeastern orchards, but with a lasting legacy as one of the two parents (along with Braeburn) of the widely marketed RubyFrost apple, to which it passed firm, dense flesh and good storage characteristics. The fruit itself is crisp and juicy with a tangy-sweet flavor, ripening in the fall and keeping reasonably well in cold storage. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator variety within range, and site it in the cold-winter apple country of the Northeast and Upper Midwest that the Geneva breeding program targets.
sources: Cornell University New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Burbank Potato (Original White-Skinned Parent of Russet Burbank)

planting.note: Plant seed potato pieces (each with 2-3 eyes) in cool soil; Burbank is a late-season variety best suited to a long, cool growing season. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat sets in; cooler zones 3-7 give the most reliable yields.

directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces in trenches 4 inches deep, hilling soil around the stems as they grow, and harvest once the vine tops die back. Burbank is the original white-skinned, smooth potato that plant breeder Luther Burbank developed and introduced from his farm in Massachusetts in the 1870s, prized in its day for its prolific yields and good cooking quality. A natural bud sport of Burbank with netted, russeted skin emerged in the late nineteenth century and was selected for superior baking and frying quality, eventually eclipsing the parent entirely under the name Russet Burbank, now the dominant commercial potato in the United States. The original smooth-skinned Burbank is rarely grown today outside of historic seed collections and potato breeding programs, having been almost entirely supplanted by its russet-skinned offspring. Cure tubers in a cool, dark location for 10-14 days before storage.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Daisy is an early-to-midseason Florida mandarin with typical mandarin cold hardiness rather than satsuma-level toughness, so give young trees a sheltered site and frost protection in zone 9a.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Daisy is a Florida-grown mandarin valued for deep orange, glossy rind and richly flavored, juicy flesh that ripens early in the mandarin season, ahead of many other Florida hybrids. It is moderately seedy when grown near other citrus and is best known today as a breeding parent behind several modern seedless University of Florida mandarin releases, including the Daisy x Seedless Kishu cross that produced Marathon mandarin. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and protect young trees from hard freezes in zone 9a.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Citrus Research and Education Center

common_name: Bowen Grapefruit (Historic Florida Parent of the Sampson Tangelo)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil. Bowen is a historic nineteenth-century Florida grapefruit grown today mainly as a curiosity by citrus historians and collectors rather than as a fresh-market fruit.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, protecting young trees from hard freezes. Bowen is a historic Florida grapefruit cultivar of nineteenth-century origin, grown today chiefly as a curiosity rather than a commercial fruit. Its lasting significance is as a parent: in 1897, USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle crossed Dancy tangerine with pollen from Bowen grapefruit at Eustis, Florida to create Sampson, the first tangelo ever produced, decades before the more familiar Orlando and Minneola tangelos followed from similar grapefruit-tangerine parentage. Give it the same deep, well-drained soil and full sun as other grapefruit cultivars, and expect standard grapefruit cold sensitivity, tolerating only brief dips into the upper 20s Fahrenheit.
